---
title: "One day, methods – the housing-audit case"
subtitle: "Four parts of ninety minutes, with a facilitator"
---
The [case study](../../cases/housing/index.qmd), which presents the original study, the Multi100 project, the five reanalyses and the SCORE replication on which every format of the case is built, is the place to start.

This is the one-day course on the housing-audit case with the methods in the foreground. It works on one field experiment, in which emails that differed only in the name that signed them were sent to public housing authorities in the United States, and on a claim of the original authors (OAs) that five analysts reanalysed for Multi100. Across the day you work as analyst no. 6. You write the estimand statement behind the claim and finish a causal graph of the experiment, reproduce one of the five reanalyses, whichever you choose, and then spend the afternoon on robustness: you work through a menu of defensible analyses, send the one that you would defend to the class chart, read the chart against the 64 specifications on the curve of the claim, and declare one analysis in a shortened preregistration template before you run it. What you leave with is a report of your own, two marks on the class chart, one explored and one declared, and the place of your result on the curve.

The day is taught mainly in the [browser lab](../../cases/housing/lab.qmd), a page of the course site on which R runs inside your browser, with nothing to install. If you have installed R and an IDE (Positron, RStudio, VS Code, etc.), the downloadable workspace holds the same tasks and gives the same numbers. The day runs as four parts of ninety minutes, with breaks of thirty, sixty and thirty minutes between them. Several of its steps are things that the class does together, such as everyone typing the value that they have just reproduced and holding it back until the facilitator says go, so the day needs a facilitator. Some stretches of the slides are optional, a short tour of the toolchain and of R in the morning and a closer look at the statistics in the afternoon, and the facilitator switches them on or off to suit the class. The same case is also taught as a [short session](../housing-short/index.qmd) and as one-day courses on [open science](../housing-one-day-open-science/index.qmd) and on [data tools](../housing-one-day-data-tools/index.qmd).

| | What happens | Length |
|---|---|---|
| [Before the day](before.qmd) | Read the case study and open the browser lab once; install R, an IDE and the workspace if you want to work there. | about an hour, more with the installation |
| [Part 1 – Credibility and tools](part-1.qmd) | What a claim is for, why the field talks of a crisis, the evidence on reproduction, robustness and replication, and the toolchain; then you get running. | 90 minutes |
| [Part 2 – The claim and its estimand](part-2.qmd) | The paper and the five analysts, estimands and the causal-graph crash course; you write the estimand statement and finish the graph. | 90 minutes |
| [Part 3 – Reproduction and exploration](part-3.qmd) | You reproduce one of the five reanalyses, then work the specification menu and put an exploratory mark on the class chart. | 90 minutes |
| [Part 4 – Multiverse, replication and preregistration](part-4.qmd) | The class reads its chart against the curve of 64, meets the replication with new data, and each participant declares one analysis, runs it and reports it. | 90 minutes |
| [After the day](after.qmd) | Where to go next in the companion curriculum. | as you like |
